sql.schema.why: The structure of the database was read: which tables exist, or which columns one has. Structure, not contents -- a run that only lists tables has not answered a question about the data.

sql.rows.incidents.why: The incident rows were read. An empty row set still counts: asking and finding nothing is knowledge, and requiring non-empty rows would let an unanswerable task burn its whole budget on a question whose answer is 'not there'.

sql.rows.repos.why: The repo rows were read -- a different fact from the incident rows even though both arrive as {"rows": [...]}. Shape alone cannot tell them apart, which is why the argument predicate exists.

sql.rows.commits.why: Commit rows were read. Not the same fact as 'how many commits': count_rows returns {"table", "count"} and is deliberately not in this type's shapes, so a run that counted commits has not read them.

sql.rows.releases.why: Release rows were read. A tag name in the question does not make a tag row a fact -- the row has to come back.

sql.rows.deps.why: Dependency rows were read, including whether they are pinned and whether they are flagged vulnerable.

sql.rows.maintainers.why: Maintainer rows were read. A handle mentioned in the goal is not evidence; the row that maps handle to repo and role is.

sql.rows.scans.why: Scan findings were read. Severity strings also appear in incidents, so the predicate names the table: the same word in two tables is two facts.

sql.rows.labels.why: Label rows were read. The join key (incident_id) lives in the rows, not in the question, so only reading them answers 'which labels'.
